definition: A tonal language is a language in which lexical tones are part of the sound system, so pitch patterns belong to stored tone categories that speakers use when learning and producing words. In the packet, Mandarin and Cantonese are examples.

reasons: The packet does not provide a general definition of what a “tonal language” is (e.g., that lexical tones are part of the sound system, or that pitch patterns map to stored tone categories for producing words).

The packet only uses the term descriptively in the context of the study (Mandarin and Cantonese as tonal languages) and discusses tone learning outcomes, perception vs. production, and “mental representations”/“tonal categories,” but it does not state the requested definition claims.
The specific phrasing about pitch patterns belonging to “stored tone categories” and being used for learning/producing words is not explicitly supported in the packet.

The definition adds unsupported details about “stored tone categories” and about speakers using them “when learning and producing words”; the packet only supports that lexical tones are relevant in speech and in tone learning, not this fuller account.

The packet supports Mandarin and Cantonese as examples, but the broader definitional claim that a tonal language is one “in which lexical tones are part of the sound system” is not explicitly stated in the source packet.
